unit.title: Perform levelling and alignment of machines and engineering components

summary: This unit teaches you to set machines level on their foundations and to line up shafts, couplings and pulleys so that they run smoothly and last. You will learn to work safely with isolated and lifted machines, to use precision levels, straightedges, feeler gauges and dial indicators, to find and correct soft foot, to align a motor to a pump with shims and jacking bolts, to align belt pulleys, to prepare foundations and fix machines down, and to record your readings.

blocks.p: Machines are built to work in straight lines and true planes. A lathe bed must be level and untwisted to turn parallel work; a motor and pump joined by a coupling must turn on one centre line. **Levelling** sets a machine's reference surfaces level on its foundation. **Alignment** lines up two shafts, a shaft and its bearings, or two pulleys, so that they run true.

Poor levelling and alignment are among the commonest causes of vibration, worn bearings, leaking seals, broken couplings and wasted electricity. In Jamaica you will meet this work on water pumps at hotels, apartment blocks, farms and water supply stations, on air compressors and fans, and on machine tools in workshops and factories.

**Who it is for:** trainees on the Welding Level 2 programme at HEART/NSTA Trust centres and other training centres. Fabricators often build machine bases and stands, and help to install, level and align the machines that sit on them.

head: What you must be able to do
What this means on the job
rows: Work safely
Isolate, lock off, tag and prove the machine dead; lift and support loads safely; keep guards in place; refit them before the machine runs.
Choose and check the tools
Use and check a precision level, straightedge, feeler gauges, dial indicators, micrometer, plumb bob, laser or optical level and torque wrench.
Prepare foundations and bases
Check the foundation, mark out, set foundation bolts and packers, clean, grout and fix down.
Level a machine
Read a precision level along and across a reference surface, work out the shims needed, and shim the low feet.
Find and correct soft foot
Check every foot with a dial indicator or feeler gauges, and shim to remove it.
Align shafts
Rough align with a straightedge and feeler gauges; take rim-and-face dial readings; work out and make the corrections.
Align belt drives
Check pulleys with a straightedge or string, correct them, and set the belt tension.
Fix down and check
Tighten bolts in a crossing pattern to the set torque, and take readings again.
Record and hand over
Record as-found and as-left readings, refit guards, and hand over for an authorised first run.

ul: A **multiple-choice theory paper** on why levelling and alignment matter, tools, shims, soft foot, types of misalignment, rough and dial indicator alignment, corrections, fixing down, foundations, belt drives, safety and records.

A **written paper** with short answers (terms such as shim, TIR, non-shrink grout, torque wrench, plummer block, pinch bar, danger tag, mm/m, thermal expansion, spider, micrometer, surface plate, safe working load) and longer answers in full sentences.

**Practical tasks** in a group: levelling a fabricated machine base or stand with a precision level and shims; and aligning a motor and driven shaft coupling with feeler gauges and dial indicators on the Centre's rig, which stays locked off throughout.

blocks.note: This work is measured in **hundredths of a millimetre**. A hair is about 0.05–0.1 mm thick. Practise reading your instruments until you are quick and sure, and always write readings down as you take them.
blocks.label: Tip

head: Problem
What it causes
rows: Machine not level, or its bed twisted
Slides bind and wear unevenly
The machine cannot cut or produce parts accurately
Oil runs to one end of the slides
Shafts out of line at a coupling
The coupling forces the shafts to bend on every turn
Vibration and noise
Hot, worn and failed bearings
Leaking seals
Worn or broken coupling inserts; even cracked shafts
More electricity used for the same work
Belt pulleys out of line
Belt wears on one edge, gets hot and squeals
Belt jumps off the pulleys
Wasted power and faster bearing wear
Soft foot or pipe strain
The machine's frame is bent when its bolts are tightened
Bearing housings are distorted, so the shaft runs out of true
Alignment that changes every time the bolts are touched

blocks.p: Good levelling and alignment give **longer machine life, fewer breakdowns, better quality work, quieter running and lower power bills**.

blocks.note: A **flexible coupling** (for example a jaw coupling with a rubber spider) allows for a little misalignment, but it does not make misalignment harmless. The forces still reach the bearings and seals, and the insert wears out quickly. Align to the maker's limits whatever the coupling.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Agree the work with the person in charge of the machine
Switch off at the machine and at the isolator
Fit your **own lock** and a **danger tag** (with your name and the date) to the isolator; in a group, use a lock-off hasp so every member fits a lock
**Prove it dead:** try the start button to show the machine will not start, then return the switch to off
Release stored energy: close the pump's valves and let the pressure out of the pipework; block anything that could move or fall
Only now remove the coupling or belt guard

ul: Keep your lock on until the work is finished, the guards are back, and everyone is clear.
Never remove someone else's lock or tag.
Use jacks, slings, eyebolts and lifting gear that are **rated** for the load (marked with their **safe working load, SWL**) and have been checked.
Lift heavy machines with a crane, hoist or the right jack, never by hand or on forklift forks left holding it up.

**Never put your hand or fingers under a machine held up only by a jack or a bar.** A jack can slip or sink. Raise the machine, put solid support blocks under it, lower it onto the blocks, and only then fit shims.
Keep fingers clear of **pinch points**: between a foot and the base, between coupling halves, and between a bar and the machine as it moves.
Use a **pinch bar** (pry bar) only in small, controlled moves, with a firm grip and good footing.

head: Hazard
Control
rows: Dropped machines, tools and parts
Safety boots
Flying particles, springing shims and bars
Safety glasses
Sharp edges on shims and burrs
Gloves when handling shims and steel, but **no gloves near anything that can turn**
Laser level beam
Never look into the beam or aim it at anyone's eyes; follow the warning label for its class
Trips over tools, cables and shims
Keep tools and shims in a tray, off the floor
Hot pump casings and pipes
Let them cool; check before you touch

ul: Refit the **coupling or belt guard**: a turning coupling catches clothing and hands.
Remove all tools, indicators and brackets from the machine.
At the Centre, the **assessor or instructor** checks the guard and set-up and decides when an aligned machine may be run for the first time. At work, the person in charge does this.

blocks.p: A **precision (engineer's) level** has a very sensitive bubble vial with graduations. It is much more sensitive than a builder's spirit level. Its **sensitivity** is given in **millimetres per metre (mm/m)** for each division: for example **0.02 mm/m** means that when the bubble moves one division, the surface slopes 0.02 mm in every metre of length.

ul: Slope (mm/m) = number of divisions the bubble moves × the sensitivity.
Height difference (mm) = slope (mm/m) × length (m).
The bubble always moves **towards the high end**.
Clean the surface and the level's base; set it on the machined reference surface the maker names; let the bubble settle before you read it.
A **frame (square) level** has accurate faces on its sides as well, so it can also check vertical surfaces.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: Level sensitivity 0.02 mm/m. The bubble moves 3 divisions.
A bed 2 m long slopes 0.05 mm/m.
One end is 0.05 × 2 = **0.10 mm** lower than the other
Sensitivity 0.02 mm/m; bubble 5 divisions towards the tailstock end; feet 1.5 m apart.
Slope = 5 × 0.02 = 0.10 mm/m; the headstock end is low
Height difference = 0.10 × 1.5 = **0.15 mm**: raise the headstock-end feet by 0.15 mm

blocks.h: Checking the level itself: the reversal test

flow: Set the level on a flat surface and note the reading (how many divisions, towards which end of the surface)
Turn the level **end for end** on exactly the same spot
Read it again
If the level is true, both readings show the same slope: the same number of divisions, towards the same end of the surface
If they differ, the level is out: the true slope is the **average** of the two readings, and the level's own error is half the difference. Have it adjusted

blocks.note: Heat bends the reading of a sensitive level. In a hot Jamaican yard, sun on one end of the level or the machine, or the warmth of your hand, can move the bubble. Shade the level, handle it by its insulated grips, and let it settle before reading.
blocks.label: Jamaica

head: Tool
Use
rows: Straightedge
A precision steel bar with a true edge; laid across coupling rims or pulley faces for rough alignment
Feeler gauges
A set of thin steel blades of known thickness; measure small gaps. The right blade **slides in with a light drag**: not forced, not loose. Blades can be added together.
Taper gauge
A tapered blade marked in thickness; measures the gap between coupling faces quickly
Dial indicator (dial test indicator)
Shows small movements of its plunger, usually in 0.01 mm divisions; used for soft foot checks and rim-and-face alignment
Magnetic base and alignment brackets
Hold dial indicators rigidly; a bracket must be **rigid**, and its **sag** must be known
Outside micrometer
Measures shim thickness to 0.01 mm
Plumb bob
A pointed weight on a line; shows a true vertical, for setting columns upright
String line
A tight line between two points, for checking long runs and pulleys
Laser level or optical level
Transfers heights over long distances, for example to set two machine bases far apart at the same height
Surface plate
A flat, accurate cast-iron or granite table used as a reference surface for checking parts, straightedges and levels
Torque wrench
Tightens bolts to a set tightness (torque) shown on a scale
Jacking bolts
Bolts in lugs on the base that push the machine's feet sideways (or lift them) in small, controlled steps
Pinch bar
A long steel bar for moving a heavy base a small amount by leverage
Hydraulic jack and support blocks
Raise a machine to fit shims; the blocks carry the load

blocks.p: **Shims** are thin metal plates placed under machine feet to raise them and set the height.

ul: Use **stainless steel** (or brass) shims, which do not rust in a damp or humid workshop. Never use cardboard, wood, plastic or drink-can metal: they squash, rot or corrode.
Pre-cut **slotted shims** slide round the hold-down bolt without removing it. They come in set thicknesses (for example 0.05, 0.10, 0.25, 0.50, 1.00 and 2.00 mm), stamped on each shim.

Use **as few shims as possible** under each foot (many workplaces allow no more than three or four). A tall stack of thin shims behaves like a spring: it squashes and settles, so the height and alignment change.
Shims must be **clean, flat and free of burrs**. File off burrs before fitting; dirt or a burr under a foot causes soft foot.
Check the thickness of an unmarked shim with a micrometer.

flow: Check the drawing and the maker's data: the machine's size and weight, the fixing points, and the foundation the maker asks for
Check the concrete: strong enough, **cured** for the time the engineer or maker gives (often several weeks for full strength), flat, and not cracked or sinking
Mark out the machine's position and bolt holes from fixed reference lines, so it lines up with other equipment
Set the **foundation bolts** (anchor or hold-down bolts): cast in, set in pockets left in the concrete, or drilled and fixed with anchors
Clean the surface where grout will go and roughen it; remove dust, oil and loose material
Set levelling pads, packing plates or jacking screws at the fixing points
Lift the machine into place with rated lifting gear, set it on the packers, and level it
Tighten the bolts lightly and check the level again

blocks.p: Large machines and base frames are often **grouted**: a special filler is poured into the gap between the base and the concrete, so the base is supported evenly along its whole length, not just at the packers. It must be a **non-shrink grout** (cement-based or epoxy), because ordinary mortar shrinks as it sets and leaves gaps under the base.

ul: Mix and place it exactly as the maker says, with forms (dams) round the base to hold it.
Pour from one side so air is pushed out, not trapped.
Let it cure for the stated time before fully tightening the foundation bolts.
Then tighten the bolts to the set torque and check the level once more.

Tighten in a **crossing (diagonal) pattern**, in **stages** (for example about a third of the torque, then two thirds, then full), not one bolt fully at a time and not round the base in order. This pulls the machine down evenly without twisting it.
Use a **torque wrench** set to the maker's figure, so every bolt gets the right tightness. Too loose and the machine moves; too tight and the bolt stretches or the foot distorts.
Pull the torque wrench steadily by its handle, and stop as soon as it clicks or reaches the set reading. Do not use it to undo tight nuts.
**Tightening can move a machine.** Always take the level or alignment readings again after the bolts are tight.

flow: Isolate the machine if it can be driven; check the foundation is solid and clean; clean the feet and pads
Check the precision level by the reversal test
Place the level on the reference surface the maker names (bed ways or table), **along** the length
Read it, and note how many divisions and which end is high
Repeat **across** the width, at both ends of the bed, to find twist
Record the as-found readings
Work out the height difference from the reading, the level's sensitivity and the distance between the feet
Raise the low feet safely with a jack or jacking screw, and **support them on blocks**
Fit clean, flat shims of the right thickness under the low feet, using as few as possible
Lower the machine and read the level again in both directions; repeat until within the limit
Tighten the hold-down bolts in a crossing pattern, check again, and record the as-left readings

blocks.p: A long bed can be level along each side and still be **twisted**: one corner high and the opposite corner low. Readings **across** the bed at the headstock end and at the tailstock end show twist: if they differ, the bed is twisted. Correct it by raising one corner foot until the cross readings agree, then check along the bed again.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: A foot must rise 0.15 mm. Shims come in 0.05, 0.10, 0.25 and 0.50 mm.
Use one 0.10 mm and one 0.05 mm shim: **two shims**, not three 0.05 mm shims
A foot must rise 0.75 mm.
One 0.50 mm and one 0.25 mm shim (two shims), rather than three 0.25 mm shims
A foot must rise 1.35 mm.

blocks.note: Write the shims you fit under each foot on the record sheet as you go. If the level reading does not change by the amount you expected, check for a burr, dirt or a soft foot before you add more shims.
blocks.label: Tip

sections.title: Shaft alignment: misalignment, soft foot and rough alignment

head: Type
What it is
Checked by
rows: Parallel (offset)
The two shaft centre lines are parallel but not on the same line: one shaft is higher, lower or to one side of the other
A straightedge across the coupling rims; rim readings with a dial indicator
Angular
The centre lines meet at an angle, so the coupling faces are not parallel
The gap between the coupling faces at top, bottom and sides; face readings with a dial indicator
Combined
Both at once; this is what you usually find
Both checks

blocks.p: Misalignment is checked in two planes: **vertical** (up and down, corrected with shims under the feet) and **horizontal** (side to side, corrected by moving the machine sideways).

One machine is the **fixed** machine and is not moved; the other is the **movable** machine. A pump bolted to fixed pipework is the fixed machine, so the **motor** is moved. Before aligning, check that the pump is firmly bolted down and that the pipes are not pulling on it (**pipe strain**): loosen the pipe flange bolts with a dial indicator on the pump coupling. If the pump moves noticeably, the pipework must be supported or corrected first, or the alignment will be lost when the pipes are bolted up.

**Soft foot** means one or more feet of a motor or pump do not sit flat on the base. When the bolt on that foot is tightened, it bends the machine's frame. This distorts the bearing housings, puts the shaft out of true, causes vibration, and makes the alignment change every time the bolts are loosened. Always check and correct soft foot **before** aligning, because no alignment reading can be trusted while the frame is being bent.

head: Kind of soft foot
What you find
Cure
rows: Parallel gap
The foot sits above the base with an even gap
Shim the gap
Angled gap
The gap is wider at one side of the foot
Stepped shims, or have the foot machined flat
Dirt, rust, burrs or paint
Something under the foot holds it up
Clean and file the foot and base
Induced (from outside)
Pipe strain or a bent base pulls the foot
Correct the pipework or base

flow: Tighten all the hold-down bolts
Set a dial indicator on the base with its plunger on the top of one foot, and zero it
Slacken that foot's bolt and watch the indicator
If the foot rises more than the limit (often about 0.05 mm, or the maker's figure), that foot is soft. Feeler gauges at the four corners of the foot show the shape of the gap
Re-tighten, and check each foot in turn
Clean, shim the gap, and test again until every foot is firm

blocks.h: Rough alignment with a straightedge and feeler gauges

blocks.p: Rough alignment brings the shafts close enough for dial indicators to be used. With the machine isolated and the guard off:

ul: **Offset:** lay a straightedge across the rims of both coupling halves, at the top and at one side. If it rests on one half and there is a gap over the other, the shafts are offset. Measure the gap with feeler gauges.

**Angle:** measure the gap between the coupling faces with feeler gauges or a taper gauge at the top, bottom and both sides. If the gap is wider at the top than at the bottom (or at one side than the other), the shafts meet at an angle.
Turn both shafts together and check again, so that an out-of-true coupling does not mislead you.
Make the rough corrections, then go on to the dial indicators.

blocks.p: A rigid bracket is clamped to one shaft or coupling half. Two dial indicators on it touch the **other** coupling half: one on its **rim** (outside edge) and one on its **face**. As both shafts are turned together, the **rim indicator** shows the **offset** between the shafts and the **face indicator** shows the **angle** between them.

flow: Isolate and lock off; remove the guard; correct soft foot; do the rough alignment

Check the bracket's **sag**: mount it on a straight bar or pipe, zero the rim indicator at the top, turn it to the bottom and note the reading (for example −0.04 mm). Allow for this in the bottom readings
Fit the bracket and both indicators, with the plungers part-way in so they can read both ways
Set both dials to zero at the top (12 o'clock)
Turn **both shafts together, by hand**, a quarter turn at a time, and record the readings at 3, 6 and 9 o'clock. Never turn the shafts by bumping the motor
Check that the readings make sense, then work out the corrections

ul: **TIR** means **total indicator reading**: the full swing of the needle, from its lowest to its highest reading, as the shafts turn.

The actual **offset** between the shaft centres is **half the rim TIR**, because the indicator travels right round the coupling: top to bottom it sees the offset twice. A rim TIR of 0.40 mm means the shafts are 0.20 mm apart.

**Validity check:** for readings taken all the way round, **top + bottom = side + side** (within about 0.02–0.03 mm). If they do not add up, a bracket has slipped, a plunger has stuck or a reading was misread: take them again.
Face readings show how far apart the faces open at one side compared with the other: the bigger the difference across the face, the bigger the angle.

head: Worked example: rim readings (sag allowed for)
Working
rows: Top 0.00, 3 o'clock +0.12, bottom +0.30, 9 o'clock +0.18 mm
Validity: top + bottom = 0.00 + 0.30 = 0.30; sides = 0.12 + 0.18 = 0.30. The readings add up
Vertical offset = 0.30 ÷ 2 = **0.15 mm**
Horizontal offset = (0.18 − 0.12) ÷ 2 = **0.03 mm**

blocks.note: Which way a reading tells you to move the motor depends on where the bracket and indicators are mounted and how the dial reads. Your instructor will show you the sign rule for the Centre's rig and record sheet. Many workshops use an alignment worksheet or calculator to work out the moves.
blocks.label: Remember

flow: Correct **soft foot** first
Correct the **vertical** alignment with shims under the motor's front and back feet (angle and offset)
Correct the **horizontal** alignment by moving the motor sideways with the **jacking bolts**, watching the dial indicators
Tighten the hold-down bolts in a crossing pattern to the set torque
Take a full set of readings again; repeat the corrections until the readings are within the limits
Record the as-left readings and the shims at each foot; refit the guard

blocks.p: Vertical is done before horizontal because the motor must be lifted and its bolts loosened to change shims, and that can shift it sideways. Moving it sideways last, with the shims in place, keeps both corrections.

head: Worked example
Working
rows: **Offset only.** The motor's shaft is 0.15 mm low, and the faces are parallel.
Raise all four motor feet by the same amount: add **0.15 mm** of shims under each foot (for example 0.10 + 0.05)

**Angle only.** The face gap is 0.20 mm wider at the top than at the bottom, measured across a 100 mm diameter. The motor's front feet are 150 mm, and its back feet 400 mm, from the coupling face. The motor's back end is low.
The slope is 0.20 mm in 100 mm
This tilts the motor about the coupling, closing the gap at the top without changing the offset there
**Both.** Work out each correction and add them at each pair of feet.
With the two examples above: front feet 0.30 + 0.15 = **0.45 mm**, back feet 0.80 + 0.15 = **0.95 mm** up

ul: Loosen the hold-down bolts just enough for the motor to slide.
Push the feet with the **jacking bolts** in small steps, watching the rim and face indicators at the side position. Back off the jacking bolt on the other side first.
Move the front and back of the motor by different amounts to correct a horizontal angle, as the readings show.
Where there are no jacking bolts, a pinch bar can be used with care, in small moves.
How close the alignment must be is given in the **maker's manual or the job specification**. Use those figures.

The **faster** the machine runs, the **closer** the alignment must be. On Jamaica's 50 Hz supply a 2-pole motor runs at about 2900 rpm and a 4-pole motor at about 1450 rpm. As a rough guide only, many tables allow about 0.05–0.10 mm offset for a 4-pole motor with a flexible coupling, and less for a 2-pole motor.

Metal grows as it heats up (**thermal expansion**). A pump handling hot water, or a machine that runs hot, grows taller when it reaches working temperature. The maker may therefore give **cold alignment figures that are not zero**, so that the shafts line up when the machine is hot.

flow: Isolate and lock off the drive; remove the belt guard; clean the pulley faces
Lay a straightedge, or stretch a string line, across the faces of both pulleys
If they are in line, it touches each pulley at **two points**, at the front and back of its rim: **four points** in all (allow for any difference in pulley width)
A gap at one point shows a pulley that is offset or at an angle; check also that both shafts are level and parallel
Correct by loosening the motor's hold-down bolts and moving or turning the motor on its base, or by moving a pulley along its shaft, until the straightedge touches all four points
Tighten the bolts and pulley set screws
Set the belt tension as the belt or machine maker says, then check the alignment again
Refit the guard before the drive is run

head: Sign
Likely cause
rows: Belt wears on one edge, or one side is shiny
Pulleys offset or at an angle
Belt jumps off or turns over in the groove
Pulleys badly out of line, or belt too slack
Squealing on start-up
Belt too slack, or worn and glazed
Hot bearings, short bearing life
Belt too tight, or pulleys out of line

ul: Too slack: the belt slips, squeals, glazes and gets hot.
Too tight: it overloads the motor and pulley bearings and shortens the belt's life.
Set it as the maker says, usually by pressing the middle of the span with a set force and measuring how far it deflects (a common guide is about 16 mm per metre of span).
When fitting several V-belts on one drive, fit a matched set, all new together. Never lever belts over the pulley rims: move the motor in to fit them.

blocks.p: Levelling and alignment work is always **recorded**. The record shows what condition the machine was in (**as found**), proves that it was put right to the required limits (**as left**), and helps the next person: if the readings change over time, something is moving, such as a sinking foundation or a pipe pulling on the pump.

head: An alignment record contains
Example
rows: Machine name, number and location
Pool pump P2, plant room
Date and the names of the people who did the work
12 March; T. Brown, D. Grant
Tools used
Precision level 0.02 mm/m; two dial indicators; feeler gauges
As-found readings
Level, soft foot at each foot, rim and face readings
Shims added or removed at each foot, and moves made
Front feet +0.45 mm; back feet +0.95 mm; front moved 0.05 mm towards the wall
As-left readings
Rim and face readings after tightening
Tolerance used and bolt torques
From the maker's manual
Problems found
Worn coupling spider; cracked grout; pipe strain
Signatures
The person who did the work, and the supervisor who checked it

ul: Remove all tools, indicators and brackets; count your tools.
Refit the coupling or belt guard.
Clean the area; put shims, tools and instruments away, instruments in their cases.
Remove your lock only when the work is finished and everyone is clear.
Hand over to the person who authorises the first run, and report anything that still needs attention.

blocks.p: Use this checklist to test yourself. If you cannot honestly say "I can" to a line, go back to that section and practise it with your instructor.

ul: I can explain why machines must be level and shafts aligned, and what goes wrong when they are not.
I can isolate, lock off, tag and prove a machine dead before working on it.
I can raise a machine safely and support it on blocks, never putting my hands under a load held only by a jack.
I can check a precision level by the reversal test and read it correctly.
I can work out a slope and a height difference from a level reading, and choose shims.
I can use feeler gauges, a straightedge, a dial indicator, a micrometer, a plumb bob and a torque wrench.
I can explain parallel and angular misalignment and check each with a straightedge and feeler gauges.
I can find soft foot with a dial indicator and correct it.
I can set up rim-and-face dial indicators, allow for sag, and take readings at four positions.
I can work out the offset from a rim TIR, and check that readings add up.
I can correct vertical alignment with shims and horizontal alignment with jacking bolts, in the right order.
I can tighten hold-down bolts in a crossing pattern to the set torque, and check the readings again.
I can explain thermal growth and why the maker's figures may not be zero.
I can align belt pulleys and set belt tension.
I can describe how a foundation is prepared, and why non-shrink grout is used.
I can complete an alignment record with as-found and as-left readings.

terms: Alignment
Lining up two shafts, a shaft and its bearings, or two pulleys so they run true
Angular misalignment
Shaft centre lines that meet at an angle
As found / as left
The readings before the work, and after it is finished
Danger tag
A label on a locked-off isolator showing who is working on the machine
Dial indicator
An instrument that shows small movements of its plunger, usually in 0.01 mm
Feeler gauge
A set of thin blades of known thickness for measuring small gaps
Foundation bolts
Bolts set into the foundation to hold a machine down; also called anchor or hold-down bolts
Isolation
Cutting a machine off from its power so it cannot start
Jacking bolts
Bolts on a base that push a machine sideways in small steps
Levelling
Setting a machine's reference surfaces level on its foundation
Non-shrink grout
A filler poured under a machine base that does not shrink as it sets
Parallel (offset) misalignment
Shaft centre lines that are parallel but not on one line
Pinch bar
A long steel bar used to move a heavy base by leverage; also called a pry bar or crowbar
Pipe strain
Pipework pulling on a pump and moving it out of line
Plumb bob
A pointed weight on a line that shows a true vertical
Plummer block
A bearing housing bolted to a base; also called a pillow block
Precision level
A sensitive engineer's level graduated in mm/m
Rim-and-face method
Alignment with one dial indicator on the coupling rim and one on its face
Safe working load (SWL)
The largest load a sling, jack or lifting device may carry
Sag
The bending of an indicator bracket under its own weight, which must be allowed for
Shim
A thin metal plate put under a machine foot to raise it
Soft foot
A machine foot that does not sit flat on its base
Spider
The rubber or plastic insert between the halves of a jaw coupling
Surface plate
A flat, accurate reference table of cast iron or granite
Thermal expansion
The growth in size of a metal part as it gets hot
TIR
Total indicator reading: the full swing of the needle as the shaft turns
Torque wrench
A wrench that tightens a bolt to a set tightness shown on a scale

c1.title: A pool pump at a hotel in Negril
c1.text: Dwight is a maintenance trainee at a hotel in Negril, Westmoreland, working with the plant-room technician, Ms Henry. The pool pump's 4-pole motor and the pump sit on a common steel base. The coupling's rubber spider is worn out and the motor bearings are noisy. The pump is bolted to fixed pipework. Ms Henry has switched off and locked the isolator, and the pump's valves are closed.

c2.title: Levelling a lathe stand in Annotto Bay
c2.text: Tashoya is a trainee at a training centre in Annotto Bay, St Mary. Her group is levelling a fabricated stand for a refurbished lathe, using a precision level with a sensitivity of 0.02 mm/m per division. Along the bed, the bubble moves 5 divisions towards the tailstock end. The feet at the headstock and tailstock ends are 1.5 m apart. The shim pack has stainless steel shims of 0.05, 0.10, 0.25 and 0.50 mm.

c3.title: Dial readings on the training rig in Williamsfield
c3.text: Orville is aligning the motor to a shaft in plummer blocks on the training rig at a centre in Williamsfield, Manchester. The rig is locked off. His rim readings, with the bracket sag allowed for, are: top 0.00, 3 o'clock +0.12, bottom +0.30 and 9 o'clock +0.18 mm. The coupling face is measured across a 100 mm diameter, and the face gap is 0.20 mm wider at the top. The motor's front feet are 150 mm, and its back feet 400 mm, from the coupling face.

c4.title: A bakery fan in Savanna-la-Mar
c4.text: Trevor maintains the equipment at a bakery in Savanna-la-Mar, Westmoreland. The V-belt on the oven's exhaust fan has jumped off twice since the motor was taken out for repair and put back. The belt is worn on one edge. With the drive isolated and the guard off, Trevor lays a straightedge across both pulley faces. It touches the fan pulley at both points of its rim, but touches the motor pulley only at its front edge.

c5.title: A new compressor in Discovery Bay
c5.text: Mr Reid's team is installing a new air compressor, with its motor on a steel skid, in a port workshop in Discovery Bay, St Ann. The concrete plinth was poured three days ago, with the foundation bolts cast in. The maker's manual asks for non-shrink grout under the skid and gives a torque figure for the foundation bolt nuts.

questions.q: Ms Henry has locked the isolator. What must be done before Dwight takes the coupling guard off?
o: Try the start button to prove the motor will not start
Turn the motor's speed control down to its lowest setting
Wait ten minutes for the motor to cool down
Ask the pool attendant to stand by the switch
questions.why: Locking the isolator is not enough on its own: the test proves that the right isolator was locked and the motor really cannot start. The switch is then returned to off.

questions.q: When the pump's flange bolts are loosened, the dial on the pump coupling moves 0.25 mm. What should be done?
o: Nothing: pipes always pull a little on a pump
Align the motor to where the pump sits now
Have the pipework supported or corrected first
Fit a thicker spider so the coupling can take it
questions.why: The movement shows pipe strain: the pipes are pulling the pump out of line. If the motor is aligned to a strained pump, the alignment is lost again when the pipes move, so the pipework is put right first.

questions.q: When its bolt is slackened, the motor's back-left foot rises 0.15 mm. Feeler gauges show an even gap under it. What should Dwight do?
o: Tighten that bolt harder to pull the foot down
Clean under it, shim the gap and retest
Put a rubber pad under the foot to take up the gap
Leave it, since the other three feet hold the motor
questions.why: An even gap is a parallel soft foot. Tightening the bolt would bend the motor's frame; the cure is to clean under the foot, fill the gap with shims, and check that the foot no longer lifts.

questions.q: The sag check on Dwight's bracket gives −0.06 mm at the bottom. What does this mean?
o: The bracket is faulty and must be thrown away
The motor is 0.06 mm lower than the pump
The dial indicator needs a new battery
Allow for 0.06 mm of sag in bottom readings
questions.why: Every bracket bends slightly under its own weight, so the bottom reading is a little off even on perfectly aligned shafts. Measuring the sag first lets him correct the real readings.

questions.q: Which end of the stand is low?
o: The headstock end
The tailstock end
Neither: the stand is level
It cannot be told from the bubble
questions.why: The bubble always moves towards the high end. It has moved towards the tailstock, so the tailstock end is high and the headstock end is low.

questions.q: By how much must the low end of the stand be raised?
questions.why: Slope = 5 × 0.02 = 0.10 mm/m. Over the 1.5 m between the feet, the height difference is 0.10 × 1.5 = 0.15 mm.

questions.q: Which shims should Tashoya fit to raise a foot by 0.15 mm?
o: Three 0.05 mm shims
One 0.10 mm and one 0.05 mm shim
One 0.25 mm shim, filed down thinner
Fifteen sheets of thin aluminium foil
questions.why: Two shims give 0.15 mm exactly, with fewer layers than three thin ones. A few flat stainless shims stay firm; a filed shim is uneven, and stacks of thin layers or soft foil squash and settle.

questions.q: In the reversal test, the level reads 3 divisions before it is turned end for end and 1 division after, both towards the same end. What does this show?
o: The surface is level and the level is true
The bubble is sticking and needs a tap
The surface is twisted, not sloping
The level has an error and needs adjusting
questions.why: A true level shows the same slope both ways round. Different readings mean the level itself is out: the true slope is the average, 2 divisions, and the level should be adjusted before more readings are relied on.

questions.q: Do Orville's rim readings make sense?
o: Yes: top plus bottom equals the two sides added together
No: a good set of readings would all be zero
No: the 9 o'clock reading should equal the 3 o'clock one
Yes: every reading is less than 0.50 mm
questions.why: Top + bottom = 0.00 + 0.30 = 0.30, and side + side = 0.12 + 0.18 = 0.30. When the two sums agree, the bracket has not slipped and the readings can be used.

questions.q: What is the vertical offset between the shaft centres?
questions.why: The rim TIR from top to bottom is 0.30 mm, and the indicator sees the offset twice as it goes round, so the offset is half: 0.15 mm. 0.03 mm is the horizontal offset.

questions.q: To correct the angle alone, by how much must the motor's back feet be raised?
questions.why: The faces open 0.20 mm across 100 mm. The back feet are 400 mm from the coupling, so they rise 0.20 × 400 ÷ 100 = 0.80 mm (and the front feet 0.30 mm), tilting the motor about the coupling.

questions.q: The rig's motor is to be replaced with a 2-pole motor running at about 2900 rpm. How does this change the alignment needed?
o: It must be closer, because faster machines suffer more
It can be rougher, because a faster motor runs smoother
It stays the same, because the coupling is the same
It no longer matters, because the spider takes it all
questions.why: The faster a machine runs, the more damage a given misalignment does, so tolerance tables allow less at higher speeds. Always use the maker's figures for the machine.

questions.q: What does the straightedge show?
o: Both pulleys are in line and the fault lies elsewhere
The fan pulley is at an angle to the motor pulley
The motor pulley is at an angle to the fan pulley
The belt is too tight for the pulleys
questions.why: The straightedge sits true on the fan pulley, but touches the motor pulley at only one point, so the motor pulley is turned at an angle. This is why the belt wears on one edge and jumps off.

questions.q: How should Trevor correct it?
o: Grind the worn edge of the belt to make it even
Turn the motor until all four points touch
Tighten the belt until it can no longer jump off
Pack a washer behind the fan pulley to move it out
questions.why: The motor was disturbed during the repair, so it is the motor that is put back in line: loosen its bolts and turn it until the straightedge touches all four points, then tighten and check again.

questions.q: With the pulleys aligned and a new belt fitted, how should Trevor set the belt tension?
o: As tight as it will go, so it can never slip again
Loose, so the fan and motor bearings last longer
By the maker's figure for deflection at mid-span
By ear, tightening until the squeal stops
questions.why: Too tight overloads the bearings, and too slack lets the belt slip and glaze. The maker's method, pressing the middle of the span with a set force and measuring the deflection, gets it right.

questions.q: The plinth was poured three days ago. When can the team grout and fix the skid down?
o: At once, since the concrete looks hard already
After it has cured for the time the engineer gives
After the first heavy rain, which tests the plinth
Once the compressor has been run to settle it
questions.why: Concrete gains strength slowly as it cures, over weeks rather than days. Fixing down on green concrete can crack it or loosen the bolts, so follow the engineer's or maker's curing time.

questions.q: Why does the manual ask for non-shrink grout under the skid?
o: It sets fast enough to run the compressor the same day
It glues the threads of the foundation bolts
It levels the skid so no measuring is needed
Ordinary mortar shrinks and leaves gaps under the base
questions.why: Grout is there to support the base evenly along its whole length. Mortar that shrinks as it sets pulls away from the skid, leaving it supported only in places.

questions.q: When should the foundation bolt nuts be tightened to their full torque?
o: Before the grout is poured, so the skid cannot move
As soon as the grout is poured, while it is wet
After the grout cures, then recheck the level
Never: the grout holds the skid without the bolts
questions.why: The bolts are snugged lightly while the grout cures, then tightened to full torque once it has set hard. Tightening can move the skid, so the level is checked again afterwards.

questions.q: How should the torque wrench be used on the foundation bolt nuts?
o: Pull steadily and stop at the click
Jerk it hard so the nut is sure to be tight
Pull past the click to add a little extra
Use a pipe on the handle for more leverage
questions.why: A torque wrench gives the set tightness only when it is pulled smoothly by its handle and stopped at the click. Jerking it, going past the click or lengthening the handle all over-tighten the nut.

questions.q: Levelling a machine in a sunny yard, you see the precision level's bubble keep drifting. What should you do?
o: Read it quickly before the bubble moves again
Tap the vial until the bubble stops moving
Shade it and let it settle before reading
Add more shims until the bubble stops
questions.why: Sun on one end of a sensitive level, or the warmth of your hand, changes its reading. Shade it, handle it by its grips, and give it time to settle.
